summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I use myself — practice screens, grading, a vocabulary and grammar system that all have to agree on what I've actually learned so far. The interesting engineering problem is that "have I learned this word" isn't one boolean; a script can be readable in kana before its meaning is actually met, and keeping those two questions straight (and consistent across a dozen different drill types) is most of the design work.

A recent fix shows the shape of the bugs that show up in this kind of system: after a wrong answer, the review screen showed the English translation of the answer I picked, but not the correct one — so the one sentence I actually needed to understand stayed untranslated. Nothing crashed, nothing looked broken in a screenshot; it just quietly failed the one job the reveal screen has. Most of my time on this project goes into catching that category of bug — plausible-looking output that's subtly wrong — with checks that assert the actual rule instead of just checking that something rendered.

On the infrastructure side, I run a small local model server (VOICEVOX) for generating Japanese audio, and I've learned to trust it over my own expectations: a few times it "refused" a reading I was sure was right, and each time the model was correct and I had the pronunciation wrong. That turned into a rule I apply generally now — when an automated check disagrees with you, check which side is actually wrong before overriding it.
